q: A blog post says: 'Google reports that 75% of its new code is AI-generated, so AI clearly makes engineers four times faster.' Using the chapter's evidence-type lens, what is the best critique?
options: It is a randomized trial result, so it does prove speed, but only for Google's own internal tools
It comes from payroll data, so it measures hiring changes rather than how the code gets written
It is a company-reported share of output; it says nothing about review time, rework, bugs or speed
It is a government projection, so it describes a possible future rather than today's codebase
explanation: Google's 75% (Sundar Pichai, April 2026) is company-reported: the company's own metric, defined by the company and not independently checked. A share of AI-written code counts output, not review time, rework or bugs, so it cannot show a speed-up. Randomized trials measure cause and effect, payroll data shows hiring, and BLS figures are projections.

q: A manager argues: '83% of our developers use AI tools at work, so they clearly trust AI for important decisions.' Which Stack Overflow 2026 finding most directly challenges this?
options: Only about 7% trust AI for important decisions; 48% trust it when they can easily verify the output
Most developers have stopped using coding agents and gone back to general chat tools instead
Trust in AI output rose above 80% in 2026, so heavy use and high trust now move together in the survey
Only 16% use AI tools at work at all, so the 83% figure really describes hobby projects
explanation: Stack Overflow 2026 (self-reported): 83% use at least one AI tool at work, but only about 7% trust it for important decisions and 48% 'trust it when I can easily verify the output' (16% is the share who say AI handles complex tasks very well). Use is nearly universal; trust is conditional. In 2025, more developers distrusted AI accuracy (46%) than trusted it (33%).

q: Which task profile best matches the setting of METR's 2025 randomized trial, where experienced developers were slower with AI?
options: Writing a new CRUD prototype in an unfamiliar framework with few existing constraints
Generating boilerplate tests for a small module with simple, predictable interfaces
Translating a simple utility from one language to another with stable requirements
Changing a large, mature open-source codebase that the developer already knows well
explanation: METR's July 2025 trial had 16 experienced open-source developers work on 246 real issues in their own large, mature repositories: tasks took 19% longer with AI. The chapter calls this a hard setting for AI; gains are usually reported on new code, unfamiliar code and boilerplate.

q: An engineer wants to hand a decision about long-term service boundaries and organisational trade-offs entirely to an AI agent. What is the chapter's critique?
options: AI agents are weak here mainly because they cannot generate enough boilerplate to compare options
Architecture needs organisational context that is not in the repo, and no test can check it
AI-generated architecture is disallowed because coding assistants only support single-file edits
The main blocker is that AI systems cannot read existing code or architecture documentation
explanation: The chapter's 'Where to use AI' table says architecture and long-term trade-offs need organisational context that is not in the repo, and no test can check them — so use AI as a sparring partner while you own the decision.

q: Which work does the chapter say you can hand to AI (and then read the diff), rather than keep for yourself?
options: Generating regexes, SQL queries, configuration files and API glue code
Coordinating stakeholders during a production incident across several services
Choosing which product requirement not to build after stakeholders disagree
Settling long-term architecture trade-offs that depend on unwritten context
explanation: Boilerplate, scaffolding, config, regex, SQL and API glue are easy to check, so hand them to AI and read the diff (69% use AI to write code in a familiar area, Stack Overflow 2026). Incident response is assist-only, deciding what not to build stays with you, and architecture needs context no test can check.

q: A friend reads PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer and concludes: 'If I add AI to my CV, my pay will go up 62%.' What is the chapter's correction?
options: The 62% applies only to AI researchers with PhDs; software engineers see no premium at all
The 62% is payroll data on what workers were actually paid after they learned AI skills
It is an average gap in advertised salaries between ads requiring AI skills and comparable ads
The 62% is a BLS projection for 2035, so it says nothing about salaries offered today
explanation: PwC analysed more than a billion job ads (Lightcast data): ads that require AI skills offer a 62% higher salary than comparable ads (57% in the previous Barometer). These are advertised salaries averaged across sectors and countries — not a promise for any individual. The premium is for building with AI on top of strong fundamentals.

q: Which activity does the chapter describe as commoditized because AI now does it cheaply?
options: Explaining architectural trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders
Writing routine docs for straightforward code and typing boilerplate
Investigating complex production incidents across several services
Making ambiguous product decisions with incomplete requirements
explanation: §4 lists boilerplate and basic CRUD, remembering syntax, simple unit tests, translating code, routine docs and formatting as commoditized. Explaining trade-offs, incident investigation and product judgement are rising. Cheap is not worthless: you still read that code to review it.

q: What is the key difference between Level 2 (Guided) and Level 3 (Delegated task) in the chapter's ladder of AI use?
options: Level 2 uses paid tools, while Level 3 relies only on free-tier assistants for repeatability
Level 2 produces single-line completions, while Level 3 avoids repository context entirely
Level 2 lets AI open pull requests on its own, while Level 3 only asks it for syntax help
Level 2 gives the AI context to follow; Level 3 hands it a spec and a check, like a junior
explanation: Level 2: you give context (for example, 'write tests following our test patterns') and check the output. Level 3: you design and write a spec with a 'done' check (for example, 'done = these tests pass'), and the AI works like a junior engineer from it. The jumps that matter are 1 to 2 (give context) and 2 to 3 (give a spec and a check).

q: Several agents work on parts of a feature in parallel, each opening a pull request, while an engineer splits the work, sets the checks and reviews before merging. Which level is this?
options: Level 1, because the human still approves the generated code before merge
Level 2, because the agents follow repository context the engineer supplied
Level 4, because several agents work in parallel like a small team you lead
Level 3, because one agent works from a spec the way a junior engineer would
explanation: Level 4 (Agentic): several agents work on parts of a feature in parallel, each opening a pull request — 'a small team you lead'. Your role is to split the work, set the checks, review and merge. Level 4 multiplies whatever discipline you already have, good or bad.

q: After checking CEO quotes against what their companies reported next, which pattern does the chapter draw?
options: Every company that predicted AI replacement has already cut its engineering headcount sharply
Hiring changed first, and differently by company: Google grew, Salesforce held flat, Meta shrank
Companies report less output per engineer, which proves AI tools have not been widely adopted
Executive timelines proved accurate, so the 2025 'midlevel engineer' arrived right on schedule
explanation: Headlines predict replacement, but what changed first is hiring — and it differs: Google's headcount grew 7.7%, Salesforce held engineering at about 15,000, and Meta fell 15% after a ~10% layoff. Every company reports more output per engineer (company-reported), and timelines slip: the 2025 'midlevel engineer' became +30% output per engineer at Meta.

q: Which pair of company-reported facts does the chapter use to show that a high share of AI-written code has not, so far, meant fewer people at Google?
options: 75% of new code AI-generated (April 2026), while headcount grew 7.7% in the year to September 2026
25% of new code AI-generated (April 2026), while headcount fell 15% after a large layoff in May 2026
50% of new code AI-generated (October 2024), while engineering headcount stayed flat at 15,000
90% of new code AI-generated (September 2026), while new-graduate hiring doubled versus 2019
explanation: Sundar Pichai (Cloud Next, 22 April 2026): 75% of all new code at Google is AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 50% last fall. Alphabet's headcount still grew 7.7%, from 190,167 to 204,757, in the year to 30 September 2026. The 15% fall is Meta; flat engineering at about 15,000 is Salesforce.

q: A backend engineer asks whether the AI engineer role is realistically open to them. Which job-data signal in the chapter is most relevant?
options: Prompt engineer is the fastest-growing standalone title, so most AI engineers began as prompt writers
AI engineer postings fell below 2020 levels, so the title is now filled mainly by internal researchers
BLS counts AI engineer as a separate occupation and projects the job count to triple by 2035
LinkedIn 2026: AI engineer is the top-growing US title, most often filled by former software engineers
explanation: LinkedIn Jobs on the Rise 2026 (platform data): AI engineer is #1 of 25 fastest-growing US job titles; the most common previous job is software engineer, with a median of 3.7 years' prior experience. Prompt engineer as a standalone job has faded into a general skill (Wall Street Journal, April 2025).

q: Stanford's Digital Economy Lab (ADP payroll data to June 2026) finds employment of 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs 19% below its expected path. What drives the gap, and how strong is the evidence?
options: Mass firings of young engineers; the authors present it as a proven causal effect of AI
Rising pay for juniors that priced them out; it is based on a self-selected online survey
Mostly fewer hires, not more firings; the authors call it early, descriptive indicators
Economy-wide job losses across all ages; it is a BLS projection rather than measured data
explanation: 'Canaries in the Coal Mine?' uses payroll data — the strongest evidence so far. The gap comes mostly from fewer hires, sits where AI substitutes for the work (where AI complements workers, employment is flat or rising), and there is no economy-wide job loss; experienced workers show no comparable gap. The authors call these 'early, descriptive indicators' rather than causal estimates.

q: Which reading of SignalFire's State of Talent 2026 matches the chapter?
options: New-grad hiring at big tech is back to 2019 levels, while engineering's share of hires fell
New-grad hiring is about 65% below 2019 at big tech, yet engineers rose to 55% of its hires
New-grad hiring is about 19% below 2019 everywhere, and startups hire more juniors than ever
Big tech stopped hiring software engineers entirely, while startup new-grad hiring doubled
explanation: SignalFire (venture-capital hiring data, June 2026): new-grad hiring is about 65% below 2019 at 12 large tech companies and about 76% below at early-stage startups. Engineering held up best — software engineers are 55% of big-tech hires (46% in 2019). Far fewer new-grad seats, but engineering is not collapsing. The 19% figure is Stanford's employment gap for 22-25-year-olds.

q: Which behaviour best reflects Addy Osmani's advice to juniors in The Next Two Years of Software Engineering (January 2026)?
options: Accept AI output quickly, since throughput matters more than explaining the implementation
Specialise only in prompt syntax, because fundamentals matter less in AI-assisted work
Avoid AI tools until fundamentals are mastered through years of unaided coding practice
Become AI-proficient and versatile, use AI to learn, and be able to explain every line
explanation: Osmani (14 years at Google, now at Anthropic working on Claude Code): 'Make yourself AI-proficient and versatile. Demonstrate that one junior plus AI can match a small team's output.' And: 'Use AI as a learning tool, not a crutch.' The chapter's junior strategy adds: be able to explain every line the agent writes.

q: What changed from the old '10x engineer' (around 2015) to the new one the chapter describes for 2026?
options: The edge moved from coding fast to writing clear specs, splitting work for agents and verifying
The edge moved from system design back to memorising syntax, since AI now handles architecture
The edge moved from production judgement to avoiding AI agents in favour of manual coding
The edge moved from domain knowledge to running as many AI tools at once as possible
explanation: Old 10x: codes and debugs fast, knows many frameworks; the bottleneck is writing code. New 10x: writes clear specs, splits work for agents, verifies fast; the bottleneck is deciding what to build and reviewing what was built. It is measured by correct, reviewed changes shipped, and its typical failure is lots of fast, unreviewed code.

q: Y Combinator said in March 2025 that a quarter of its Winter 2025 startups had codebases about 95% written by AI. Which lesson does the chapter draw from this?
options: Technical skill no longer matters, since non-technical founders now ship whole products with AI
Vibe coding is now the professional standard for products that handle users, data and money
Leverage still needs judgement: YC stressed these founders were highly technical, with taste
AI-written codebases are always unsafe, so YC advised its startups to stop using coding agents
explanation: YC stressed that 'every one of these people is highly technical', and partner Diana Hu added that good vibe coding still needs 'taste and knowledge to judge good versus bad' (TechCrunch, 6 March 2025). AI multiplies output only when someone can judge the result.

q: Which statement best fits the chapter's 'honest picture' of where AI helps most?
options: AI makes deep changes in huge, familiar codebases easy, but barely helps with boilerplate
AI gives the same speed-up regardless of codebase familiarity, test coverage or task type
AI helps most on security-sensitive code, where its output is both fast and reliably safe
Large gains on boilerplate, clear gains on medium features, little or none on deep changes
explanation: The chapter's table: boilerplate, glue code and tests for a clear spec — large speed-up; medium features in a well-tested codebase — clear speed-up; deep changes in a huge codebase you know by heart, or novel design — small, none or negative; security-sensitive code — fast but often unsafe. Judge leverage by correct, reviewed work shipped.

q: An engineer ships an AI-built feature that precisely follows a vague request but solves the wrong user problem. Which mistake from the chapter does this illustrate?
options: Building the wrong thing efficiently
Ignoring AI entirely
Using AI as a faster typewriter
Trusting your gut about speed-up
explanation: Mistake #2: AI speeds up whatever you aim it at — including a wrong requirement. The fix is to spend more time on requirements, acceptance tests and design, and less on typing.

q: A developer merges an AI-written input-handling function because it compiled and the demo worked. Which mistake is this, and what is the chapter's fix?
options: Ignoring AI entirely; the fix is to try one free AI tool on real tasks every day for a week
Trusting without verifying; review it like a new teammate's pull request and scan it in CI
Building the wrong thing efficiently; the fix is to spend more time on requirements and design
Becoming a prompt monkey; the fix is to switch AI off and rewrite the function by hand
explanation: Mistake #3, trusting without verifying: code that compiles is not code that is safe — about 44% of AI code-generation tasks fail security tests (Veracode 2026). Review AI output like a new teammate's pull request and run tests and security checks in CI.

q: To measure your own AI speed-up, the chapter says to estimate each task first and then flip a coin to decide whether AI is allowed. Why the coin?
options: It removes the need to log actual times, because the coin result already predicts the outcome
It guarantees a narrow confidence interval even if you only record a dozen tasks in total
It stops you from using AI only on the easy tasks, which would bias the comparison
It makes sure AI is used on exactly the hardest tasks, where the speed-ups are largest
explanation: Random assignment is the idea behind a randomized trial: if you choose when to use AI, you may pick the easy tasks and fool yourself. Then compare the mean actual/estimate ratio with and without AI. Feelings are unreliable — METR's developers were 19% slower yet felt faster — and 12 tasks give a wide interval; 4x the tasks halves it.

q: An engineer says: 'I'm a real programmer — I don't need AI tools.' Which evidence from the chapter best explains why this is a mistake?
options: AI tools now write all of Google's code, so manual coding skills are no longer tested anywhere
Google interviews now require candidates to use AI in every round, including coding rounds
Engineers who avoid AI are 7 times less likely to be hired, according to PwC's payroll data
83% of developers use AI at work, and Google requires AI fluency for all engineering roles
explanation: Mistake #6, ignoring AI entirely: 83% of Stack Overflow 2026 respondents already use AI tools at work, and a Google spokesperson said (October 2026) that AI fluency is required for all software-engineering jobs. Fix: start with one free tool on real tasks, daily. Google interviews still disallow AI outside pilot rounds, and PwC's 7x is about entry-level job ads asking for senior skills.

q: What does becoming a 'prompt monkey' mean in the chapter's list of common mistakes?
options: Following too many AI communities and newsletters without doing enough hands-on implementation
Being able to work only with AI, without the skills needed when models fail or tasks are novel
Writing prompts that are too detailed for models to follow in multi-file code changes
Focusing on system design prompts instead of using AI for autocomplete and small fixes
explanation: Mistake #7: if you can only work with AI, you are fragile — models hallucinate, tools go down, and novel problems need your own thinking. The fix: build real skills and use AI; together they are strong, either alone is fragile.

q: Which action belongs in the playbook's 'Do This Week' tier?
options: Install one AI coding tool and use it on real work rather than toy examples
Read Designing Data-Intensive Applications and pick one domain to go deep in
Build a RAG app or agent that combines software engineering and AI, with evals
Contribute to open-source AI tools or MCP servers as an ongoing career habit
explanation: Tier 1 (this week): install one AI tool and use it on real work, give your agent a short project-instructions file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md), start a one-line-per-task time log, and follow one community. DDIA, domain depth and an AI project with an evaluation set are quarter-level; open-source contributions are ongoing.

q: Which action is in the playbook's 'Do This Month' tier?
options: Pick one domain such as healthcare, finance or infrastructure and go deep in it
Move from autocomplete to the agentic loop: spec, plan, small diffs, tests, review
Shift your story from 'I write code' to 'I design systems and ship verified work'
Install one AI coding tool and follow one community such as Hacker News
explanation: Tier 2 (this month, about 30 min/day): move from autocomplete to the agentic loop of §5, build one small project end to end and explain every file, learn MCP, read three papers you can explain, and keep a 'what AI got wrong' journal. Domain depth is quarterly, the story shift is ongoing, and installing a tool is this week.

q: Which study plan is placed in the playbook's quarter-level tier rather than the week or month tier?
options: Keep a journal of every bug, hallucination or security issue that AI produced
Follow one community such as Hacker News, r/LocalLLaMA or your tool's forum
Deepen system design with Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition)
Install one free AI coding tool and use it on real work tasks starting today
explanation: Tier 3 (this quarter) includes deepening system design with DDIA (2nd edition, 2026) plus Ch 23-25, going deep in one domain, becoming AI-literate, and building an AI project with an evaluation set. The journal is a monthly habit; the community and the tool install are this week.

q: The chapter warns against two opposite myths about junior developers. Which reply rejects both, using its data?
options: No economy-wide displacement and AI-exposed entry roles grew 35%, yet new-grad hiring is far down
AI has already replaced junior developers, so founding a startup is the only path still left open
Nothing has changed for juniors; the dip in hiring is explained entirely by interest rates alone
Juniors are hired more than ever, because AI makes every one of them as productive as a senior
explanation: Myth 1, 'AI has replaced junior developers': the data shows no economy-wide displacement, and AI-exposed entry-level roles grew 35% since 2019 (PwC 2026). Myth 2, 'nothing has changed': employment of 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below its expected path (Stanford), and big-tech new-grad hiring is about 65% below 2019 (SignalFire). The door is narrower, not closed.

q: Which skill is ranked Priority 1 ('Must') in the chapter's learning-priority table?
options: Technical communication and leadership
Building AI features: RAG, agents, MCP, evals
Domain expertise in one chosen industry
AI tool fluency: specs, agents and review
explanation: Priority 1 is AI tool fluency: Google requires AI fluency for all software-engineering roles (Ch 2 §1.4), and 68% of developers expected employers to require AI-tool proficiency soon (JetBrains, 2025). System design and CS fundamentals are the other two 'Musts'; building AI features is 'High'; domain expertise and communication are 'Medium'.

q: Why are CS fundamentals still a 'Must' in the learning stack even though AI can produce code?
options: Fundamentals are mainly needed to memorise APIs that AI tools cannot suggest reliably
Fundamentals guarantee that AI-generated code will never contain any security vulnerabilities
You cannot debug what you do not understand, and AI amplifies rather than replaces knowledge
AI tools require engineers to implement operating systems and networking layers by hand
explanation: The learning stack lists CS fundamentals (DSA, OS, networking) as a 'Must' because you cannot debug what you do not understand. AI amplifies what is already there; it does not replace understanding — so sometimes switch AI off and write key algorithms by hand.

q: Your team adopted a coding agent. Pull requests per week went up, and so did failed deployments. According to DORA 2025, what is happening and what should you fix first?
options: The agent is defective; switch to another vendor's model and keep the process unchanged
AI amplifies what is there; fix the system with smaller batches, strong tests, fast feedback
Throughput and stability always rise together, so the failures must be unrelated to AI
Reviews are too slow; approve AI pull requests faster so that the backlog clears sooner
explanation: DORA 2025 (Google Cloud; nearly 5,000 professionals) found AI adoption goes with higher delivery throughput and lower delivery stability: 'AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there.' More changes hit weak testing and review, so fix the system — smaller batches, strong automated tests, fast feedback loops and clear review rules — not the tool.

q: A colleague 'vibe codes' a customer-facing payments feature, accepting every change without reading the diffs. How does the chapter distinguish this from agentic engineering?
options: They are the same practice; 'agentic engineering' is just a newer marketing name for it
Vibe coding uses agents, while agentic engineering forbids agents in favour of autocomplete
Vibe coding is safe for payments if the code compiles; agentic engineering is for prototypes
Vibe coding suits throwaway projects; agentic engineering keeps quality via tests, CI, review
explanation: Karpathy coined 'vibe coding' on 2 February 2025: accept every change, don't read the diffs — 'not too bad for throwaway weekend projects'. In February 2026 he proposed 'agentic engineering' for professional work: claim the leverage of agents 'without any compromise on the quality of the software'. You read every line you merge, and tests, CI and review decide 'done'. Anything with users, data, money or security needs the latter.

q: Which combination matches the chapter's final formula for an engineer whom AI makes stronger, not replaceable?
options: Strong fundamentals, AI fluency, system design and domain expertise
Prompt fluency, framework memorisation, daily tool use and typing speed
Deep ML research, cloud certifications, startup experience and UI taste
Autonomous agents, code volume, social media presence and job hopping
explanation: The formula: strong fundamentals (you can debug what AI writes) + AI fluency (clear specs, good context, checks) + system design (you decide what gets built) + domain expertise (you know what 'correct' means).

q: How should you use the BLS Employment Projections 2025-35 for software developers in an interview answer?
options: As measured payroll data proving AI has had no effect on software jobs since 2025
As a projection of about +10% growth: a direction, not precision, since projections move
As proof the profession will shrink, since the 2025-35 projection is negative for developers
As a company-reported figure that Google published alongside its AI-written code share
explanation: BLS projects software developers, QA analysts and testers to grow 10% from 2025 to 2035 — almost three times the 3.5% for all jobs; software developers go from 1.72 to 1.89 million, about 175,000 more jobs. The previous round (2024-34) said +15.8%. It is a projection whose assumptions can be overtaken by events — read it as direction, not precision.

q: Which scenario best illustrates the rising value of domain expertise in the chapter?
options: An engineer memorises every API in a web framework to avoid needing generated code
A generalist asks AI to build CRUD screens without knowing the product's compliance rules
A finance engineer uses industry knowledge to judge whether AI logic fits regulatory rules
A developer accepts generated pull requests without reading the business requirements
explanation: The rules of health care, finance or infrastructure are rarely written where a model can read them. Domain experts know what 'correct' means, so they can judge whether AI output fits real constraints — AI is general; your context is not.

q: Why does the chapter say verification and code review are rising in value, citing DX data?
options: AI code needs no tests, so code review is now the only quality gate a team has left
The median pull request grew from 44 to 72 lines in a year, so there is more to check
AI-written pull requests are always shorter, so reviewers can now handle many more
Reviewers only need to check formatting, since models now handle edge cases reliably
explanation: DX measured the median pull request growing from 44 to 72 lines between July 2025 and June 2026 — more code for a human to review. More AI code means more to check: write the test first and review every AI diff as if a new hire wrote it.

q: A teammate says: 'We use a coding-specialised model, so we can skip security scanning.' What does Veracode's 2026 report show?
options: Coding-specialised models passed 100% of security tasks, so scanning is redundant for them
Security pass rates doubled since 2025, so only older models still need code scanning
Only Java code had flaws; Python code from coding models passed every security test
Coding-specialised models scored 51% vs 52% for general ones — no safer; scan everything
explanation: Veracode 2026 (raw models, 100+ models): average security pass rate 56%, so about 44% of tasks produced code with a known flaw — 'virtually unchanged' since 2025 — even though about 100% of the code compiled. Coding-specialised vs general-purpose: 51% vs 52%. By language: Python 63% … Java 30%. Treat AI code like any unreviewed code: scan it, fix it, never ship it blind.

q: Compared with 'fix the discount bug', why is the chapter's Level 3 prompt for the 100% discount crash better?
options: It asks for a failing test first, names edge cases, keeps the signature and defines done
It lets the agent edit as many files as it likes, so the bug gets fixed in fewer turns
It tells the agent to skip tests so the fix can ship before the checkout outage spreads
It is longer, and longer prompts always make models more accurate whatever they say
explanation: The Level 3 prompt names the function and file, asks for a failing test that reproduces the crash, adds edge cases (0%, 20%, over 100%), forbids changing the function signature and says 'Done = all tests pass'. The Level 1 prompt lets the agent guess, edit several files and report 'done'.

q: You assign an issue to a tool that works in a cloud sandbox and later opens a pull request for you to review. Which of the chapter's four tool shapes is this?
options: IDE assistant / AI editor
Terminal agent
Cloud / async agent
Agent manager
explanation: Cloud / async agents take an issue, work in a cloud sandbox and open a pull request (for example GitHub Copilot assigned an issue, Codex cloud tasks, Devin Cloud). Terminal agents edit files and run commands in your shell; agent managers supervise several agents in parallel; IDE assistants work inside your editor. Learn the shapes, not the brands.

q: In November 2026, a student with a free personal Google account wants Google's terminal coding agent. Which tool does the chapter point them to?
options: Gemini CLI, which still serves free individual accounts with unchanged limits
Antigravity CLI, which replaced Gemini CLI for individual accounts in June 2026
Jules, Google's cloud coding agent, which opened free student sign-ups in 2026
Gemini Code Assist, which became Google's only free tool for terminal coding
explanation: Gemini CLI and the Gemini Code Assist IDE extensions stopped serving free and Google AI Pro/Ultra individual accounts on 18 June 2026 and were replaced by Antigravity CLI (enterprise licences and API keys are unaffected). Jules is winding down: read-only after 11 November 2026 and closing on 31 December 2026.

q: Your coding agent reads GitHub issues and web pages while it works. One issue contains hidden text telling the agent to upload secrets. What is this risk, and what is the chapter's main defence?
options: Hallucination; fix it by asking the model to double-check its own answer before acting
Vibe coding; fix it by reading the diffs, since the agent wrote code nobody reviewed
Prompt injection (OWASP LLM01); give the agent only the least privilege it needs
Model drift; fix it by retraining the model on the team's own repository every week
explanation: Agents add a new attack surface: prompt injection, where text hidden in a web page, issue or file that the agent reads tells it what to do (OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM01). Give agents the least privilege they need, and keep scanners and human review in the loop (Ch 17b §5.11, Ch 18b §18.14).

q: In 2026 Windsurf became Devin Desktop, Cursor became part of SpaceX, Kiro replaced Amazon Q Developer and Jules began closing. What lesson does the chapter draw?
options: Learn the tool shapes and one solid workflow, because brand names change every few months
Pick one vendor early and stay with it, because switching tools wipes out all prior skills
Avoid AI coding tools until the market settles, because product names will stop changing
Use only open-source agents, because commercial tools cannot be trusted to keep existing
explanation: Brand names change every few months: Windsurf became Devin Desktop (2 June 2026), Cursor joined SpaceX (deal closed 14 August 2026), Kiro replaced Amazon Q Developer (from 15 May 2026) and Jules closes on 31 December 2026. So learn the four shapes and one solid workflow — spec, plan, small diffs, check, review — not one product.

q: In the Spec step of the agentic loop, the chapter suggests keeping a short AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md) file. What should it contain, and why?
options: A full copy of the whole codebase, so the agent never needs to open any other repository file
The team's salaries and roadmap, so the agent can make prioritisation decisions alone
A list of banned AI vendors, so the agent refuses to call any other model during a task
Build and test commands plus rules the code doesn't show, which the agent can't otherwise see
explanation: AGENTS.md is 'a README for agents': build and test commands, code style and house rules the code doesn't show (Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md). The agent cannot read decisions that live in meetings or in someone's head, so you write them down (Ch 18 §18.9).

q: Your company's agent must hand a task to an agent built by a different vendor. Which protocol from the chapter standardises that?
options: MCP (Model Context Protocol), which connects one agent to tools and data
AGENTS.md, a README file that tells coding agents how to build and test
A2A (Agent2Agent), started by Google in April 2025 for agent-to-agent tasks
ACP (Agent Client Protocol), which runs any compatible agent inside an editor
explanation: A2A (Google, April 2025) standardises how agents from different vendors hand tasks to each other. MCP (Anthropic, November 2024) is how an agent reaches tools and data; AGENTS.md gives coding agents build and test commands; ACP (Zed, with JetBrains) runs agents inside editors, like LSP did for language servers. MCP and AGENTS.md went to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation on 9 December 2025, and A2A joined in August 2026.

q: Why does the chapter say technical communication rises in value as AI handles more implementation?
options: Communication replaces the need to understand code, because AI now answers all technical questions
When implementation is fast, explaining trade-offs to people and agents becomes the bottleneck
Communication matters only for managers, because individual contributors focus on prompts
Written communication is useful mainly for documenting generated code line by line
explanation: Skill #9 in §3: when implementation is fast, explaining trade-offs to people (and agents) becomes the bottleneck. Practise with short design docs and decision records; PwC also finds AI-exposed entry-level roles 7x more likely to ask for judgement and leadership.

q: Which example best fits 'use AI as a learning tool, not a crutch' for a junior engineer?
options: Accept model output once tests pass and skip reading internals to preserve velocity
Ask AI for complete implementations only in languages the engineer does not know
Ask for hints rather than answers, read the generated code and explain why it works
Use AI on every practice problem and never switch helpers off during study sessions
explanation: Osmani: use AI as a learning tool, not a crutch. The chapter adds: when you use AI to learn, ask for hints, not answers, and be able to explain every line. AI that does your thinking can hurt learning (Ch 5 §5.11), so also solve some problems with AI switched off.

q: An engineer lets the same AI write a pricing function and the only tests for it. All tests pass. Why does the chapter call this a trap?
options: AI-written tests always fail on correct code, so a green run actually signals a hidden bug
Tests are no longer needed for AI code, so writing them only wastes the agent's token budget
Two AI outputs in one change break the agentic loop, which allows one AI step per task
Tests derived from the code check what it does, not what it should do, so they pass on bugs
explanation: §4's trap: tests generated from the code copy its bugs — they check what the code does, not what it should do. Derive tests from the spec and write the edge cases yourself; the §5 program shows a weak check accepting a wrong patch 'with a green tick'.

q: In METR's July 2025 randomized trial, how did experienced developers' beliefs compare with the measured result?
options: They expected a slowdown, felt slower afterwards, and the clock confirmed they were 19% slower
They expected to be 24% faster and still believed they were 20% faster, but took 19% longer
They expected no change, felt no change, and the measured times showed no difference at all
They expected to be 19% faster, and the clock showed they were in fact 24% faster with AI
explanation: METR (16 experienced open-source developers, 246 real issues, early-2025 tools, mostly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet): tasks took 19% longer with AI (95% CI +2% to +39%). Developers expected to be 24% faster and afterwards still believed they had been 20% faster. Feelings are unreliable — measure your own tasks.

q: METR's February 2026 follow-up found returning developers took about 18% less time with AI (CI -38% to +9%). Why does METR call this very weak evidence, yet think the true speed-up is probably larger?
options: 30-50% of developers held back tasks they did not want to do without AI, skewing the sample
Only 16 developers took part, and every one of them refused to use any AI coding tool at all
The study used self-reported times only, with no randomization of tasks between groups
Developers were paid per task, so they rushed every task they completed without AI
explanation: The follow-up (57 developers, 800+ tasks, August 2025 to February 2026) is a randomized trial, but 30-50% of developers held back tasks they did not want to do without AI, so tasks where AI likely helps most were missing and the true speed-up is probably larger. New developers showed -4% (CI -15% to +9%). The intervals cross zero: a signal, not proof. METR also believes developers are 'more sped up from AI tools now'.

q: METR reports that an agent has a 50%-time horizon of 12 hours. What does that mean?
options: The agent can run on its own for 12 hours without any human input before it stops
The agent needs 12 hours to finish tasks that a skilled human completes in 6 hours
It succeeds half the time on tasks that take a skilled human about 12 hours to do
It can do any 12-hour job in a real company, as long as a person checks it at the end
explanation: The time horizon is the task length, in human expert time, at which an agent is predicted to succeed with a given reliability — here 50%. It is not how long the agent runs (agents usually finish solved tasks several times faster than people), and not 'any 12-hour job': the tasks are self-contained, clearly specified and scored automatically.

q: GitHub Octoverse 2026 reports that more than 40% of pull requests started with an agent in September 2026. What is the main weakness of this type of evidence?
options: It is a small randomized trial, so the sample is too small to generalise to all developers
Platform telemetry counts activity such as pull requests and lines, not the value of work
It is a government projection, so its assumptions can be overtaken by later events
It is self-reported, so developers misjudge how often they start pull requests with agents
explanation: Platform telemetry logs what the tools record, at huge scale, but it counts activity (commits, lines, pull requests), not value. Surveys suffer from self-report bias, randomized trials from small samples, and projections from assumptions that change. The share was 17% in March 2026.

q: METR's trend fit for 2023 onwards gives the 50%-time horizon a doubling time of about 129 days. Roughly what growth per year does that imply?
options: About 2x per year
About 3x per year
About 4x per year
About 7x per year
explanation: h(t) = h0 * 2^(t / T) with T of about 129 days (95% CI 104-158 days): 2^(365 / 128.7) is about 7.1, so roughly x7 per year — a doubling about every four months. The chapter's program checks the trend: from Claude 3.7 Sonnet (1.0 h) it predicts 6.5 h for Claude Opus 4.6, which measured 12 h — inside METR's wide error bars.

q: Claude Opus 4.6 has a 50%-time horizon of about 12 hours but an 80%-time horizon of about 1.2 hours. What lesson does the chapter draw?
options: Reliability lags capability: errors compound over steps, so dependable tasks are far shorter
The 80% figure is a measurement error, because the two horizons should always be about equal
Agents are more reliable on longer tasks, so delegate the biggest tasks to them first
The gap shows humans are slower than agents, so the 80% horizon measures human error
explanation: The 80% horizon is about 5-10x shorter than the 50% horizon (Claude Opus 4.6: about 12 h vs 1.2 h, a ratio of about 10). Errors compound over many steps, so the task length an agent handles reliably is far shorter than the length it manages half the time (Ch 18 §18.1).

q: In the chapter's agentic loop (spec, plan, small diff, check, review), why ask the agent for a plan before any code on tasks bigger than one file?
options: An approved plan lets the agent skip the check step, since the plan already guarantees the code
A plan replaces human review, so you no longer need to read the final diff before merging
A wrong plan is cheap to fix and wrong code is not, so you fix the plan rather than the code
Plans are needed mainly for billing, since vendors charge less for planned agent sessions
explanation: Step 2 (Plan): for anything bigger than one file, ask for a plan first and fix the plan, not the code — a wrong plan is cheap to fix; wrong code is not. Then make one small step per commit, let tests, types, lint and CI check it, and read every line before you merge: once merged, you own it.

q: If METR's trend held, when would the 50%-time horizon grow from 12 hours to a 40-hour work week? What does the chapter's program conclude?
options: Exactly 224 days later; the trend is precise enough to plan a team's hiring around
In about 6 to 9 months, depending on T — so treat it as a scenario, not a forecast
Never, because the doubling has already stopped and the horizon is now shrinking
Within one week, since agents already run for 40 hours unsupervised in practice
explanation: With T = 104, 129 or 158 days, 12 h becomes 40 h after about 181, 224 or 274 days (about 6, 7 or 9 months). The date moves by three months just from the uncertainty in T, and 40 h lies beyond the 16-hour range METR's tasks can measure reliably — so extrapolations are scenarios, not forecasts.

q: Challenger, Gray & Christmas reports that US employers named AI in 121,401 announced job cuts in January-October 2026. How does the chapter say to read this?
options: As payroll data proving AI caused every one of those job losses across the economy
As a randomized trial showing that AI adoption doubles a firm's layoffs within a year
As the reasons employers give in announcements, not measured causes of the cuts
As a BLS projection of how many software jobs will disappear by the year 2035
explanation: Challenger counts employer announcements: AI was named in 121,401 announced cuts in January-October 2026 (about 20% of announced cuts), up from 54,836 in all of 2025, and economic conditions overtook AI as the top stated reason for 2026. These are the reasons employers give, not measured causes; payroll and résumé data are stronger evidence.

q: What is the chapter's stance on how deeply a non-ML software engineer must learn how AI works?
options: They must become ML engineers before using AI coding tools professionally
They can ignore AI internals because tooling abstractions handle model behaviour
They should replace system design study with transformer architecture deep dives
They do not need to become ML engineers, but they must become AI-literate
explanation: Tier 3 of the playbook: you don't need to become an ML engineer, but you must be AI-literate (Ch 17, Ch 17b). The learning table ranks 'How AI works: transformers, embeddings, RAG, fine-tuning' as High priority — know a tool's limits before you trust it.

q: Which quarter-level project does the playbook recommend to combine software engineering and AI?
options: A RAG app, an agent or an AI feature in an existing product, built with an evaluation set
A compiler written by hand without any AI help, to prove raw coding speed to employers
A static portfolio page that lists every AI tool and model the developer has tried
A benchmark spreadsheet comparing vendor claims without building any application
explanation: Tier 3: build something that combines software engineering and AI — a RAG app, an agent, or an AI feature in an existing product — with an evaluation set (Ch 17c §4). It shows AI product integration, which Google asks for in most roles above entry level.

q: A candidate preparing for Google asks whether they may use AI tools during interviews, and how to show 'AI fluency'. What does the chapter say?
options: AI is allowed in every round, so practise prompting Gemini instead of solving problems yourself
AI is not allowed except in pilot rounds that provide Gemini; prepare a story of using AI well
AI fluency is not assessed at Google, so the topic can be skipped entirely during preparation
Candidates may bring any AI tool they like, as long as they disclose it to the interviewer
explanation: Outside pilot rounds in which candidates use Gemini to read, debug and optimise code, AI is not allowed in Google interviews. Because Google says AI fluency is required for all software-engineering jobs (October 2026), prepare one story about using AI tools well and checking their output, plus one past project you can discuss in depth (Ch 2 §1.4).

q: How does the learning-priority table relate AI tool fluency and system design?
options: Both are 'Must': AI fluency is required at Google, and deciding what to build is still not cheap
AI tool fluency replaces system design, because agents now make all the long-term architecture calls
System design is downgraded to 'Medium', because code generation now dominates engineering
Both rank below prompt-engineering skills and memorising model APIs in the priority table
explanation: Priority 1 is AI tool fluency (Google requires AI fluency for all software-engineering roles) and Priority 2 is system design and architecture ('code is cheap; deciding what to build is not'). They complement each other; neither replaces the other.

q: According to the chapter's final formula box, who is 'doing well' and who is 'at risk'?
options: Doing well: maximise AI code volume and cut review; at risk: anyone writing tests by hand
Doing well: senior engineers only; at risk: everyone in entry-level roles, whatever their skill
Doing well: tool-agnostic generalists; at risk: anyone who goes deep in one industry domain
Doing well: use AI daily and deepen fundamentals; at risk: ignore AI or trust it unchecked
explanation: The formula box: 'Doing well: use AI every day AND keep deepening fundamentals. At risk: ignore AI entirely, OR trust it without checking.' Start today with one action from §11 and one AI-free problem a week.

q: In the context of staying relevant, what is 'brain fog'?
options: A formal neurological disease that shows up clearly on an MRI scan and always needs medication
A type of burnout that affects only engineers over 40 after many years of on-call rotations
Slow internet that makes AI tools laggy and breaks concentration during pair programming
Not a diagnosis: a group of symptoms such as poor focus, mental fatigue and slow recall
explanation: Brain fog is not a medical diagnosis but an everyday name for symptoms — trouble concentrating, mental fatigue, forgetfulness, slow thinking — usually temporary, with causes from short sleep and stress to medical conditions (Cleveland Clinic, 2024). It matters because it degrades judgement and the review of AI output first.

q: Which everyday AI-era workflow most directly taxes focus through 'attention residue'?
options: Switching between IDE, chat, agent and Slack all day, so part of your mind stays on the last task
Writing one complex function in a single uninterrupted block with all notifications turned off
Reading one research paper slowly from start to end without opening any other browser tabs
Taking a quiet walk away from the screen so that a hard problem can settle in the background
explanation: After a switch, part of your mind stays on the old task — 'attention residue' (Leroy, 2009); in office studies interrupted work was resumed about 23 minutes later on average. Protect one 60-120-minute single-task block, and if forced to stop, write a one-line 'ready-to-resume' note (Leroy & Glomb, 2018).

q: A colleague cites the MIT Media Lab preprint 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' as proof that AI damages the brain. What is the chapter's measured reply?
options: It is a large peer-reviewed trial, so it settles the question: avoid AI tools while learning
It is an early warning, not proof: small, not peer-reviewed, and its EEG analysis is disputed
It found ChatGPT users had the strongest brain connectivity, so AI use is clearly beneficial
It studied only sleep and caffeine, so it says nothing at all about how people use AI tools
explanation: Kosmyna et al. (2025): 54 adults wrote essays with ChatGPT, a search engine or no tool while wearing EEG; the ChatGPT group showed the weakest connectivity and often could not quote their own essays. But it is small (18 people in the key fourth session), not peer-reviewed as of November 2026, and a written critique questions its EEG analysis. Lesson: use AI, but keep doing the hard thinking yourself.

q: An engineer says six hours of sleep a night is enough because they feel fine. Which finding does the chapter use to answer this?
options: Extra sleep fully replaces exercise, water and regular meals as a way to stay mentally sharp
Most engineers lose no attention on 5 hours a night if they drink enough coffee during the day
6 hours a night for 2 weeks caused lapses like up to 2 nights without sleep, barely noticed
Sleep affects only long-term memory, not attention or the careful reviewing of code
explanation: Van Dongen et al. (2003): 6 hours a night for 2 weeks caused attention lapses like up to 2 nights without sleep — and people barely noticed. Sleep 7+ hours with a fixed wake time, alongside movement (WHO: 150-300 minutes of moderate activity a week), water and regular meals.

q: In a randomized trial with about 1,000 students (Bastani et al., PNAS, 2025), what happened with plain GPT-4 help, and what does the chapter conclude?
options: Practice and exam scores both rose by 48%, so AI should do all of the practice work for students
Scores did not change in any group, so AI has no effect on how people learn or perform later
Practice scores fell 17% but exam scores rose, so struggling with AI builds long-term skill
Practice rose 48% but later unaided exams were 17% worse; attempt first, use AI as a tutor
explanation: Plain GPT-4 help raised practice scores 48% but left students 17% worse on a later exam without AI; a hints-only tutor largely avoided the harm. If AI does the thinking, you get the output but not the practice — so attempt hard problems yourself, ask for hints rather than answers, and keep regular AI-free reps.

q: Brain fog has lasted for weeks despite good sleep and daily movement. What does the chapter advise?
options: See a doctor: sleep apnoea, low thyroid, B12 deficiency or depression are common, treatable causes
Push through it, since brain fog always clears on its own within a day or two whatever the cause
Quit all AI tools permanently and write every line of code by hand from that point onward
Raise caffeine intake steadily until the fog clears, even if that means coffee late at night
explanation: See a doctor if fog lasts for weeks despite good sleep and movement, or gets in the way of daily life — sooner with worsening memory, low mood for 2+ weeks, or loud snoring and gasping at night. Common, treatable causes include sleep apnoea, an underactive thyroid, vitamin B12 deficiency, depression or anxiety, chronic stress, medication side effects and long COVID (Cleveland Clinic; NHS).
